# About this document {#sec-about .unnumbered}

FastAPI turns a Python function into a web service. The function gets an
address, such as `POST /predict`, and FastAPI reads the types of its arguments
and of its return value as the contract of the service: it checks every
request against them, turns the JSON of the request into Python objects and the
result back into JSON, and documents the service from them. Almost everything
that FastAPI does, and what it lets through, follows from that (@sec-model).
Working with it comes down to writing the functions and their types, then
running, calling, and testing the service (@sec-usage).

A service brings a model or a computation to users who call it over the
network, from any language, at the price of running it for as long as it
exists ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-web)). The science belongs in a
library that the service calls, not in the service itself. A service usually
runs in a container ([](../containers/docker.qmd#sec-service)).

Checked against FastAPI 0.153, Pydantic 2.14, and Uvicorn 0.54.


# How FastAPI thinks {#sec-model}

A request passes through three layers. A server, Uvicorn, receives it from the
network and hands it to the application, which FastAPI builds from the
functions; FastAPI finds the function for the method and the path of the
request, checks and converts the data on the way in and on the way out, and
the server sends the answer back:

```default
client    POST /predict   {"pressure_kpa": 101.3, "n_atoms": 12}
server    Uvicorn receives the request and passes it to the app
app       FastAPI finds the function for POST /predict
          checks the JSON against Sample           422 if it does not fit
          calls predict(sample)                    500 if it raises
          turns the Prediction into JSON
client    200   {"melting_point_k": 412.7, "model_version": "1.2.0"}
```

The status code says how a request went: 200 for success, 422 for a request
that does not fit the contract, with a message that names the field, and 500
for an exception in the function.


## The types are the contract {#sec-contract}

The types of a function are written as models of Pydantic: classes that list
the fields of the request and of the response, with their types, their
constraints, such as `Field(gt=0)`, and their descriptions. FastAPI rejects
every request that does not fit before the function runs, so the function
never sees a negative pressure or a missing field
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-validation)). It also documents the
service from them, at `/docs`, in a page where every field shows its type, its
constraints, and its description, and where requests can be tried out. Put the
units into the descriptions, or into the names of the fields, such as
`pressure_kpa` ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-conventions)).


## What the contract lets through {#sec-lax}

By default, the contract is lenient in three ways, and each can turn into a
plausible wrong number:

- **Unknown fields are ignored.** A request with a misspelled field, such as
  `temperatur`, passes, and the function computes with the default of
  `temperature` instead ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-no-guess)).
  `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` in a model rejects such a
  request.
- **Values are converted.** The string `"101.3"` is accepted as a float and
  `12.0` as an integer. `ConfigDict(strict=True)` accepts only values of the
  right type.
- **JSON has no NaN.** FastAPI turns NaN and infinity in a response into
  `null`, the same as a missing value, so a client cannot tell them apart. Give
  missing values a documented meaning, and do not return infinities
  ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-missing)).


## One server, many requests {#sec-concurrency}

The server runs many requests at once. A function defined with `def` runs in a
pool of threads, so a slow one does not hold up the others. A function defined
with `async def` runs in the loop that serves all requests, and must never
compute or wait without `await`: a prediction in it stops every other request
until it ends. Define functions that compute with `def`.

A service loads its model once, when it starts, in the function `lifespan`
(@sec-app), not in every request, which would make each slow. `--workers 4`
starts four processes, and each loads its own copy of the model and keeps its
own memory: a cache or a counter in a variable exists four times, and what one
process writes the others never see. A computation that takes minutes does not
fit into a request, which clients and proxies cut off after some time; such a
service returns an ID for the job at once and the result when it is asked
again.


## Every answer carries its version {#sec-version}

A service changes under its users, so a result has to record the version that
produced it ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-web)). Return the version of
the code and of the model in every response, as `model_version` does in
@sec-app, and give the service its version in `FastAPI(version=...)`, which
`/docs` shows. A change that breaks clients gets a new path, such as
`/v2/predict`, while the old one keeps working for a while
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-stable-api)).


# Working with FastAPI {#sec-usage}

The example serves a model that predicts melting points, saved with joblib; a
model registered in MLflow loads by its version instead
([](../tracking/mlflow.qmd#sec-models)).


## Write a service {#sec-app}

```python
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

import joblib
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

model = {}


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    model["regressor"] = joblib.load("model.joblib")    # once, at startup
    yield


app = FastAPI(title="Melting points", version="1.2.0", lifespan=lifespan)


class Sample(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    pressure_kpa: float = Field(gt=0, description="Pressure, in kPa")
    n_atoms: int = Field(gt=0, description="Atoms per molecule")


class Prediction(BaseModel):
    melting_point_k: float = Field(description="Melting point, in K")
    model_version: str


@app.post("/predict")
def predict(sample: Sample) -> Prediction:
    x = [[sample.pressure_kpa, sample.n_atoms]]
    value = float(model["regressor"].predict(x)[0])
    return Prediction(melting_point_k=value, model_version=app.version)
```

`lifespan` runs the code before `yield` when the service starts and the code
after it when it stops. `Sample` is the contract of the request and
`Prediction` that of the response: FastAPI checks the request against the type
of the argument, and the response against the return type, which also keeps
any field out of the response that `Prediction` does not list. `@app.get`
serves requests that only read, such as `GET /health`; their arguments are of
simple types and come from the address, as in `GET /stations?country=NO`.


## Run it {#sec-run}

```bash
fastapi dev main.py                # at 127.0.0.1:8000, reloads on change
fastapi run main.py --workers 4    # for production
```

`fastapi dev` serves on the machine itself and restarts the service whenever
the code changes, for development. `fastapi run` serves on every network
address of the machine, `0.0.0.0`, as a container needs; on a server outside a
container, a web server in front of it, such as nginx, handles encryption and
logins. Both start Uvicorn and serve the documentation at `/docs`. In a
Dockerfile, `CMD ["fastapi", "run", "main.py"]` starts the service.


## Call it {#sec-call}

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"pressure_kpa": 101.3, "n_atoms": 12}'
```

Any language calls the service with an HTTP library, such as httpx or requests
in Python and httr2 in R, and the page `/docs` tries out requests in the
browser. `/openapi.json` describes the whole service in the OpenAPI format,
from which tools generate clients in other languages.


## Test it {#sec-test}

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from main import app


def test_rejects_an_unknown_field():
    with TestClient(app) as client:          # runs the lifespan
        response = client.post(
            "/predict",
            json={"pressure_kpa": 101.3, "n_atoms": 12, "temperatur": 300},
        )
    assert response.status_code == 422
```

`TestClient` sends requests to the application in the same process, without a
server or a network, so tests of a service run with pytest like any other.
Use it in a `with` block: without one, `lifespan` does not run, and the model
is never loaded. Test the contract, such as that unknown fields and negative
pressures are rejected, and test the science in the library that the service
calls, not through the service.
